subject: occuTTD error: "initial value in vmmin is not finite"

messages.author: 9743508ad656e4da
messages.subject: occuTTD error: "initial value in vmmin is not finite"
parts:
Good day everyone,

I am attempting to run a time-to-detection analysis using occuTTD, in an effort to assess determinants of reptile occupancy in different habitats on a nature reserve. The pilot dataset consists of two survey replicates of 21 sites that were searched for 90 minutes each. Sixteen habitat variables were measured at each site, of which 13 were retained for further analysis.

When I attempt to fit the model using occuTTD, I encounter a persistent error:



Altering the initial values using the starts component of occuTTD had no effect, and the error arises in various subsets of the data.

I see this error was recently raised in a gmultmix example. Has anyone encountered it in occuTTD before? I would greatly appreciate any feedback on this issue.

Kind regards,

Kurt

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: occuTTD error: "initial value in vmmin is not finite"
parts:
It can be hard to narrow down the reason for this type of error. A couple suggestions: first, you should not be referencing the site and obs covs in the actual formulas, so e.g. your detection formula should just be

~temp+rel_hum+daily_rain+twoday_rain.

Second, I would strongly suggest starting with intercept-only models and building up to more complex models, in order to identify when specifically the error begins to occur. You are trying to estimate a very large number of parameters from what is ultimately fairly limited data (TTD), and it may simply not be possible to extract that much information.

Ken

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: A comment on model complexity in occupancy and similar models
parts:
Hi all,

this is a comment motivated by a recent post on this list where a model with 10 or so covariates was fit to occupancy data from 20 sites. This is asking FAR too much from the data !

We should never forget that a static occupancy or Nmix model can be viewed as the combination of two regression models: one for occupancy/abundance and the other for detection. So, we can only estimate so many parameters from so much data. In the general regression literature one can find rules of thumb that for every parameter in a regression model, one needs, say, 5-10 data points. So this would then suggest that with 20 sites, one should estimate at most 4 parameters in the state model. This could be one intercept plus 3 slopes for instance.

But the situation is even worse: while in a simple regression, these data points are observed, in a regression for occupancy probability, the implied data points are the latent presence/absence states of each site. These are not even observed, or only partially so (in the no-false-positive models we assume that the 1's are observed); rather, we must estimate the data points in the model. So we have even less information. This might then suggest that in a model fit to 20 sites we should perhaps not estimate more than 2 or 3 parameters in the state model at most.

We are in a slightly better situation for the observation model. Due to the repeated-measures nature of the data, there is more information on the detection part of the model; plus, the data are actually observed rather than partially latent. Hence, with 20 sites and, say, 3 visits at each, our sample size relevant for estimation of detection is 60, and then we may try to fit perhaps up to 5-10 parameters in the observation model.

I admit that I have disregarded these recommendations myself from time to time. But I think they are important as a benchmark when working with these models.

Best regards  -- Marc
